Tiras
tī'ras
n. (seventh and last-named son of Japheth, head of a nation the Bible names once and never follows)
From Hebrew Tiras, of uncertain derivation; the ancient association is with the Aegean sea-peoples. Scripture gives the name and no more, and the dictionary does not manufacture what the text withholds.

Biblical Definition

Tiras closes the roll of Japheth's sons: “Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras” (Gen 10:2), repeated word for word by the Chronicler a thousand years later (1Ch 1:5). That is the whole of him. No sons are listed, no land assigned, no prophecy spoken over him, no later mention anywhere in the canon. He is a man whose entire scriptural existence is a name in a column — and that is worth an entry, because it teaches something the fuller genealogies cannot. Genesis 10 is not a list of the peoples who would matter to Israel; it is a census of the whole post-flood race, and it includes the branches that leave no trace in the covenant narrative. The chapter's closing verse says so: “These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations: and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood” (Gen 10:32). Tiras is counted there. The God who numbers the hairs of a head numbers the nations too, including the ones history forgets, and Paul will say that He determined “the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26) for every one of them — Tiras included, though no man now can point to the map and say where.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Tiras; in sacred history he is the seventh son of Japheth, named in the table of nations and nowhere else.

expand to see more

TIRAS, n. The last named of the seven sons of Japheth.

He is mentioned in Genesis and repeated in the first book of Chronicles, in the same order.

No posterity, territory or history is assigned to him in the sacred text.

Ancient writers connected the name with the sea-faring peoples of the Aegean, but Scripture is silent.

The name stands as one of the seventy from whom the nations of the earth were divided after the flood.

Key Scripture

Gen 10:2 — "The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras."

1Ch 1:5 — "The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras."

Gen 10:5 — "By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands; every one after his tongue, after their families, in their nations."

Gen 10:32 — "These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations: and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood."

Modern Corruption

A name with no attached history invites two opposite abuses — filling the silence with confident identifications the text does not support, or treating the silence as proof that the list is fiction.

expand to see more

The first abuse is speculative. Because Tiras is bare, writers have hung whole theories on him — this or that ancient sea-people, this or that modern nation, sometimes with prophetic charts attached. The dictionary declines. Scripture gives a name in a genealogy; where God has not spoken, confident speech is not faith but presumption, and the man who builds an end-times map on an unidentified son of Japheth has left the ground of revelation. Deuteronomy draws the line: “The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever” (Deu 29:29). Tiras belongs, for now, largely to the first clause.

The second abuse is dismissal. Because the name is untraceable, the whole table is filed as folk memory rather than record — a literary construct organized around the number seventy. But an invented list is exactly the thing that does not carry dead weight. A composer building a symbolic genealogy supplies each name with a function; a record preserves names whose bearers left no mark, because they were there. The Chronicler copies Tiras unchanged into a work written for a returned remnant with no conceivable interest in him, which is what men do with archives and not with allegories. The dictionary treats Genesis 10 as history because it reads like history at exactly the points where invention would have improved it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Tiras (H8494), Tiras; toledoth (H8435), generations, genealogical record; mishpachah (H4940), family, clan; goy (H1471), nation.

expand to see more

Hebrew Tiras (H8494) — Tiras; the seventh son of Japheth, of uncertain derivation.

Hebrew toledoth (H8435) — generations, begettings; the structural word that frames Genesis and marks its records as records.

Hebrew mishpachah (H4940) — family, clan; the unit by which Gen 10:32 divides the nations.

Hebrew goy (H1471) — nation, people; the seventy of Genesis 10 and the Gentiles of the prophets.

Hebrew 'iy (H339) — isle, coastland; the region assigned to the sons of Japheth.

Usage

"“And Meshech, and Tiras” — the last name in the column, and the last we hear of him."

"“By these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood” — the untraceable branch is counted with the rest."

"A name without a history is still a name God saw fit to preserve."
